items.title: How a Compass Actually Finds Magnetic North
items.content_text: A compass needle aligns with Earth's own magnetic field, not true north, which is why every accurate reading needs a small correction called declination.

items.title: How a Defibrillator Actually Restarts a Stopped Heart
items.content_text: A defibrillator doesn't restart a flatlined heart — it delivers a brief, powerful shock that stops chaotic electrical activity so the heart's own natural rhythm can resume.

items.title: How a Fire Extinguisher Actually Fights Different Fires
items.content_text: A fire extinguisher doesn't just spray water — it breaks one leg of the fire's chemical triangle, and using the wrong agent on the wrong fuel can make a fire far more dangerous.

items.title: How a Hologram Actually Stores a 3D Image on a Flat Surface
items.content_text: A hologram doesn't record a picture — it records an interference pattern of light waves, letting a flat piece of film somehow show a scene from different angles.

items.title: How a Jet Engine Actually Generates Thrust
items.content_text: A jet engine sucks in air, compresses it, burns fuel to expand it violently, then blasts it out the back — Newton's third law does the rest.

items.title: How a Kaleidoscope Turns a Few Beads into Endless Patterns
items.content_text: A kaleidoscope holds a handful of loose beads and mirrors, yet never repeats. The trick isn't the beads — it's how mirror angles multiply one glimpse into endless symmetry.

items.title: How a Mars Rover Navigates Without Real-Time Human Control
items.content_text: No one on Earth can drive a Mars rover with a joystick — the delay is too long, so it looks at the ground itself and decides, in real time, whether it's about to fall off a cliff.

items.title: How a Nuclear Reactor Actually Generates Electricity
items.content_text: A nuclear reactor splits uranium atoms to release heat, which boils water into steam that spins a turbine — the reaction never touches the electricity-generating machinery.

items.title: How a Parachute Actually Slows a Falling Body
items.content_text: A parachute doesn't stop gravity — it trades a small canopy for a huge one, turning a compact skydiver into a wide, slow-falling shape air resistance can balance against weight.

items.title: How a Pressure Cooker Actually Cooks Food Faster
items.content_text: A pressure cooker doesn't just trap heat — it traps steam until pressure rises high enough to push water's boiling point far above 100°C, which is the entire secret to its speed.

items.title: How a Seismograph Actually Measures an Earthquake
items.content_text: A seismograph doesn't feel the ground shake — it exploits a mass's inertia, letting the earth move around a motionless weight while a sensor records the difference.

items.title: How a Smoke Detector Actually Tells Smoke From Clean Air
items.content_text: Most home smoke detectors don't smell smoke — they watch a beam of light or a stream of ions, and the two designs catch fires at genuinely different speeds.

items.title: How a Submarine Actually Controls Its Buoyancy
items.content_text: A submarine dives and surfaces by flooding or emptying ballast tanks with seawater, adjusting its own weight until it exactly balances the water it displaces.

items.title: How an X-Ray Machine Actually Sees Inside the Body
items.content_text: X-rays pass easily through soft tissue but are absorbed by dense bone, so the machine isn't seeing directly — it's photographing a shadow of whatever blocked the beam.

items.title: How Bats Actually See the World Through Echolocation
items.content_text: A bat doesn't listen for sound in the dark — it shouts constantly and reconstructs an entire three-dimensional world purely from the timing and pitch of what bounces back.

items.title: How Espresso Extraction Actually Works
items.content_text: Espresso isn't just strong coffee — it's a specific extraction forcing near-boiling water through compacted grounds at 9 bars, pulling out a chemical mix no drip method can.

items.title: How Glaciers Actually Carve Valleys and Move Downhill
items.content_text: A glacier isn't a frozen, static block — it's a slowly deforming river of ice that flows under its own weight, grinding rock and carving valleys over thousands of years.

items.title: How the Eiffel Tower Actually Grows Taller in Summer
items.content_text: The Eiffel Tower physically grows up to 15 centimeters on hot summer days — not an illusion, but simple thermal expansion acting on 7,300 tons of sun-heated iron.

items.title: How Velcro Actually Grips With Thousands of Tiny Hooks
items.content_text: Velcro isn't sticky at all — it's two different woven surfaces, one bristling with tiny hooks and one made of soft loops, with grip that comes purely from mechanical snagging.

items.title: Why a Boomerang Actually Flies Back to the Thrower
items.content_text: A returning boomerang isn't spinning magic — it's a fast-spinning wing whose two arms generate uneven lift, and that imbalance steadily steers the whole flight path into a curve.
